_meta.nome: Cathedrals and Basilicas of the World
_meta.descricao: A curated selection of historically or architecturally notable cathedrals, basilicas and churches around the world — not an exhaustive directory of parishes.
_meta.aviso: This collection of cathedrals and basilicas is continually expanded and is not yet a definitive or exhaustive catalog: the Church does not maintain a closed list of all its places of worship in the world. For catechetical or editorial use, always check the primary source cited in each entry.
_meta.revisao_editorial: Completion dates without historical consensus are marked with 'c.' (circa) or have been omitted. No data was estimated or filled in by inference.
fontes_gerais: GCatholic.org (directory of minor and major basilicas)

itens.resumo: The largest Gothic cathedral in Germany, built over more than 600 years to house the relics of the Magi.
itens.corpo:
The history of Cologne Cathedral begins, in practical terms, in 1164, when Archbishop Rainald von Dassel — archchancellor and trusted man of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa — brought to the city the supposed bones of the Three Magi, taken from the Basilica of Sant'Eustorgio in Milan as spoils of war after the imperial sack of the Lombard city. Overnight, the modest Carolingian cathedral of Cologne, unable to hold the crowds of pilgrims that the possession of the relics attracted, became too small for its new status as one of the greatest pilgrimage shrines of European Christendom. Between 1190 and 1225, the goldsmith Nicholas of Verdun and his workshop made the Shrine of the Three Kings for the relics, a casket in the form of a basilica covered in gold and silver and studded with more than a thousand precious stones and ancient cameos, still considered today the greatest piece of medieval sacred goldsmithing in Western art.

It was to house this reliquary worthily that Archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden laid, on August 15, 1248, the foundation stone of the new Gothic cathedral, inspired by the great French cathedrals of Amiens and Beauvais. The choir, the first part of the building to be completed, was consecrated in 1322 and received the shrine of the Magi in its interior. The works, however, proceeded slowly over the following centuries and were in fact halted in 1560: the Gothic style had fallen out of use in the face of Renaissance taste, and the Protestant Reformation and then the Thirty Years' War drained resources and interest in completing the church. For almost three centuries the cathedral remained with only half of its south tower built, topped by a medieval wooden crane that, motionless for generations, paradoxically became a picturesque symbol of the Cologne skyline — appearing in engravings and travelers' accounts as a curiosity of the city.

The decisive impetus to resume the works came from the German Romantic movement of the 19th century, which rediscovered the Gothic Middle Ages as an expression of a German national identity yet to be unified. Scholars such as Sulpiz Boisserée located and published, in the 1810s, the original medieval plans of the façade, until then believed lost, which made it technically possible to complete the building exactly as it had been conceived in the 13th century. In 1842, King Frederick William IV of Prussia personally laid the foundation stone for the resumption of the works, treating the project as a cause of national prestige and combining Prussian state funding with civic associations supporting the cathedral (the Dombauvereine, still today responsible for part of the building's maintenance). Under the direction of the architects Ernst Friedrich Zwirner and later Richard Voigtel, the work advanced following the recovered medieval drawings to the letter, and on October 15, 1880, the finial cross of the south tower was finally put in place, completing, more than 600 years after the start of construction, the largest Gothic church in Germany and, for a brief period, the tallest building in the world, with its towers of 157 meters.

The cathedral went through the Second World War under Allied bombing that struck it fourteen times, even suffering the direct impact of incendiary bombs and heavy artillery; even so, its Gothic structure of buttresses and flying buttresses withstood, and the building remained standing amid the near-total destruction of Cologne's historic center around it — a fact that fostered, in the city, the perception of the cathedral as a symbol of resilience. Structural repairs extended for decades after the war. Declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 — a distinction that was even put at risk in 2004, when the organization placed the cathedral's surroundings on the list of endangered sites because of nearby skyscraper projects, reversed after negotiation with the city authorities —, the Kölner Dom is today the most visited monument in Germany, receiving about six million people a year. Behind the high altar, the Shrine of the Three Kings continues to receive pilgrims, keeping alive, more than 850 years later, the devotion that gave rise to one of the greatest cathedrals in the world.

With its two twin towers of 157 meters, a body 144 meters long by 86 wide and an interior area of almost 7,000 m², Cologne Cathedral was, at the moment of its completion in 1880, the tallest building in the world, a title it lost a few years later to other constructions but which illustrates the scale of the Gothic undertaking resumed in the 19th century. The main façade, adorned with 108 gargoyles that also serve the practical function of rainwater drainage spouts, is today considered one of the largest church façades on the planet. The church houses eleven altars and receives about twenty thousand visitors daily, which consistently makes it the most visited monument in Germany — ahead even of secular tourist attractions such as the Brandenburg Gate. The long history of interruptions and resumptions of the work fostered, among the people of Cologne, a popular saying according to which, when the cathedral is finally declared "completely finished," it will be a sign of the end of the world — a legend that reflects how much the idea of a work in eternal completion has become part of the city's identity.

itens.resumo: The largest Gothic cathedral in the world, built on the site of a former Almohad mosque, it holds the tomb of Christopher Columbus and the Giralda tower.
itens.corpo:
Seat of the Archdiocese of Seville — historically known as Magna Hispalensis —, the cathedral occupies the site of the city's great aljama mosque, built between 1172 and 1198 under the Almohad caliphs Abu Yaqub Yusuf and Yaqub al-Mansur, when Seville was the capital of the Almohad empire on the Iberian Peninsula. After the Christian reconquest of 1248 by Ferdinand III, the mosque was converted into a cathedral church and remained so for over a century, until, by then in poor condition, the cathedral chapter decided in the early fifteenth century to demolish it and build a temple worthy of the city. Gathered in the Corral de los Olmos, the chapter is said to have declared in 1401 its intention to build "a church so great and of such quality that those who see it finished will take us for madmen" — a phrase that sums up the ambition of the project. According to tradition, the work began in 1401, but there is no documentary record of the start of the works until 1433. Among the first master builders was the Norman master Carlín (Charles Galter), who is said to have arrived in Seville fleeing the Hundred Years' War, after working on other great European Gothic cathedrals.

The progress of construction was marked by serious structural episodes. On October 10, 1506, the "last stone" was placed at the highest point of the crossing lantern, symbolically declaring the work finished, and the following year, 1507, the temple was consecrated — although some work remained to be completed. On December 28, 1511, however, one of the enormous pillars collapsed, bringing down the lantern that covered the crossing, apparently because of the excessive weight of the structure. Master Alonso Rodríguez was dismissed, and the architect Juan Gil de Hontañón designed a new dome, following the early Gothic style, completed in 1519 — which explains the discrepancy between sources that date the completion of the cathedral to 1506 and others to 1519. That same lantern collapsed again 370 years later, on August 1, 1888, and was rebuilt in the same form by the architect Joaquín Fernández. With a length of about 126 meters and an area of more than 11,500 m², Seville Cathedral is considered the largest Gothic cathedral in the world and the third largest Christian church by area, behind Saint Peter's in the Vatican and the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace of Yamoussoukro.

From the Muslim temple, the cathedral preserved two elements that are now central to its identity: the Patio of the Orange Trees (Patio de los Naranjos), the former ablutions courtyard, whose entrance gate was Christianized as the Puerta del Perdón, and the minaret, transformed into a bell tower under the name Giralda. Built from 1184 by the architect Ahmad ibn Baso — known in Christian sources as "Gever" —, the minaret originally stood about 82 meters tall, topped by four golden spheres, and instead of stairs it had a system of internal ramps wide enough for the muezzin to ride up on horseback. Between 1560 and 1568, already under Christian rule, the architect Hernán Ruiz II added to the old minaret a Renaissance bell section, crowned by the bronze statue known as "El Giraldillo": cast by Bartolomé Morel in 1568, 3.47 meters tall and weighing about 1.2 tons in the body alone, it represents victorious Faith and, by turning with the wind like a weathervane, gave the tower the name by which it is known to this day.

The Gothic interior houses the High Altarpiece of the Main Chapel, the largest Christian altarpiece in the world: begun in 1482 by the Flemish sculptor Pieter Dancart and completed around 1564 by successive generations of artists, it stands about 20 meters high and brings together more than a thousand figures carved in polychrome and gilded wood, arranged in 44 scenes from the life of Christ and the Virgin. The central choir, carved in the fifteenth century by the master woodcarver Nufro Sánchez, has 117 stalls carved with biblical and allegorical scenes, among them the king's stall, decorated in 1478 with the coats of arms of Castile and León; the organ, one of the most powerful in Spain, has more than 7,000 pipes. In the central nave, a neo-Gothic funerary monument by the sculptor Arturo Mélida, erected in the late nineteenth century, bears on the shoulders of four allegorical figures of the kingdoms of Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre a coffin with remains attributed to Christopher Columbus. The cathedral also holds the Royal Chapel, pantheon of the kings Ferdinand III — the conqueror of Seville, canonized in 1671 — and Alfonso X the Wise, as well as collections of Spanish sacred painting with works by Murillo and Zurbarán.

The attribution of Columbus's remains was reinforced by a genetic study conducted by the University of Granada. In 2003, José Antonio Lorente, a specialist in Legal and Forensic Medicine, and the historian Marcial Castro obtained authorization to open the Seville tomb, finding small bone fragments mixed with soil, which were later compared with the DNA of the navigator's son, Hernando, also buried in the cathedral, and that of his brother Diego, whose bones were in the Cartuja. The preliminary results of 2005-2006, then inconclusive and interrupted by the need to destroy bone samples, were only resumed in 2020 and released on October 12, 2024 in the RTVE documentary "Colón ADN: Su verdadero origen," in which Lorente stated that he now had "practically absolute reliability" that the remains in Seville are those of Columbus, a finding replicated by different laboratories. The same study also suggested a Western European origin for the navigator — possibly Valencia — and traits consistent with Sephardic Jewish ancestry, a thesis that reignited the debate over the traditionally accepted Genoese birthplace. Experts, however, cautioned that the conclusions were presented in a television documentary and not in a peer-reviewed scientific article, which Lorente promised to publish — which is why the finding remains a matter of controversy among Columbus historians. The cathedral was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, as part of a listed complex that includes the cathedral, the Royal Alcázar and the General Archive of the Indies, and today routinely receives more than 150,000 visitors per month, a flow that funds a substantial part of the upkeep of its monumental structure.

itens.resumo: Unfinished masterpiece of Antoni Gaudí in Barcelona, consecrated as a minor basilica by Benedict XVI in 2010 and the oldest active construction project in the world.
itens.corpo:
The Sagrada Família project began in 1882 on the initiative of a lay association devoted to Saint Joseph, under the plans of the architect Francisco de Paula del Villar, who conceived a conventional neo-Gothic church. A disagreement led Villar to abandon the work as early as 1883, and the direction of the project then passed to Antoni Gaudí, only 31 years old at the time, who completely transformed it into a project without precedent in the history of architecture. Gaudí devoted to it, with growing intensity, practically the rest of his life — from 1914 he refused to accept any other professional commission and lived literally inside the construction site, in a small room attached to the workshop. On June 7, 1926, while crossing a street in Barcelona on his way to his daily confession, he was struck by a streetcar; modestly dressed and carrying no documents, he was even mistaken for a beggar and was only identified hours later, dying three days afterward, on June 10, 1926. He was buried in the crypt of the church itself, where his tomb remains. His cause for beatification, opened by the Archdiocese of Barcelona in 1992 and formally resumed in the canonical sphere in the early 2020s, advanced decisively on April 14, 2025, when Pope Francis recognized Gaudí's heroic virtues and conferred on him the title of Venerable, leaving the cause to demonstrate a miracle through his intercession in order to attain beatification.

Gaudí conceived the temple as a true Bible in stone, a catechesis in stone intended to instruct in the faith even those who could not read: the Nativity Façade, facing east and the only one completed under his direct supervision, celebrates the birth of Christ in a profusion of plant and animal figures sculpted with almost scientific naturalism; the Passion Façade, erected decades later in a deliberately austere and angular style by the sculptor Josep Maria Subirachs, contrasts with the exuberance of the Nativity to express the suffering and death of Christ; the Glory Façade, the last and largest of the three, dedicated to the resurrection and the last judgment, is still under construction. The project provides, in all, for eighteen spindle-shaped towers — twelve dedicated to the apostles (between 98 and 112 meters), four to the evangelists (135 meters, crowned by the figures of the ox, the lion, the eagle and the angel), one to Mary and the tallest, in the center, to Jesus Christ — all crowned by polychrome ceramic elements and crosses that recover the Catalan technique of trencadís. The tower of Mary, at 138 meters, was completed on December 8, 2021, with the placing of a twelve-pointed star; the four towers of the evangelists were finished between 2023 and November of that year. Of the whole, Gaudí only saw one tower finished in his lifetime, that of Saint Barnabas, completed in 1925, a year before his death.

The work survived dramatic episodes: during the Spanish Civil War, in 1936, anarchist militiamen set fire to the crypt and destroyed a large part of Gaudí's workshop, including plaster models and original drawings that had to be reconstructed from fragments and photographs, in a technical effort that stretched over decades. When Gaudí died, only about 10 to 15% of the project had been built. Historically financed by voluntary donations — Gaudí once said that “my client is not in a hurry” —, construction gained decisive momentum from the end of the twentieth century, when millions of paying visitors made the continuous advance of the works viable, now also supported by 3D modeling technologies that translate Gaudí's complex hyperbolic geometric calculations into executable plans. Structurally, the architect started from paraboloids, hyperboloids and helicoids studied through physical models, such as the famous model of suspended strings and weights that allowed him to calculate, by inverted gravity, the ideal curvature of the arches, dispensing with external buttresses.

On November 7, 2010, Pope Benedict XVI consecrated the temple for worship and declared it a minor basilica — not a cathedral, since that function remains with the Cathedral of Barcelona —, praising it as a space of beauty, faith and hope that leads man to the encounter with Him who is truth and beauty. On February 20, 2026, with the installation of the upper arm of the cross, measuring 4.5 x 4.5 x 4.9 meters, the external structure of the central tower of Jesus Christ was completed, raised to its definitive 172.5 meters and becoming the highest point of the basilica; inside its upper arm will be placed the sculpture of the Agnus Dei, by the Italian artist Andrea Mastrovito. The tower has a twelve-sided plan and was raised in levels beginning on October 16, 2018, with prefabricated panels of pre-compressed stone combining stone and steel; the last panel was installed on December 4, 2024, at 142.5 meters. With this height, the Sagrada Família is confirmed as the tallest church in the world, respecting Gaudí's wish never to surpass the height of Mount Montjuïc, which dominates Barcelona, so as not to surpass the work of God. The interior works, however, will continue throughout 2027 and 2028, and the Glory Façade remains pending. The Nativity Façade and the crypt were inscribed by UNESCO on the World Heritage List on June 17, 2005, as part of the group “Works of Antoni Gaudí” (whose first properties, such as Park Güell and Casa Milà, had been inscribed in 1984). The basilica is also recognized by the Guinness World Records as the oldest active civil construction project in the world, with more than 140 uninterrupted years of work since the foundation stone was laid on March 19, 1882, by Bishop Josep Urquinaona.

itens.resumo: The oldest cathedral in Portugal, whose consecration in 1089 predates the very foundation of the Portuguese kingdom.
itens.corpo:
According to the tradition of the Church in Braga, the episcopal see of the city goes back to the apostle James the Greater himself, who is said to have left there as its first bishop his disciple Saint Peter of Rates — a legendary origin which, although not historically verifiable, illustrates the antiquity with which the diocese has always understood itself. Historically documented, the reconstruction of the cathedral of Braga began at the end of the 11th century, in a context of restoration of Galician-Portuguese Christendom after decades of Muslim rule and of decline of the city. The present building was consecrated and dedicated to Saint Mary by Bishop Dom Pedro in a solemn ceremony held on August 28, 1089 — a date that makes Braga Cathedral the oldest cathedral in Portugal, erected almost four decades before the Portuguese nation itself was founded, in 1128, with the Battle of São Mamede.

The importance of the Cathedral grew in parallel with that of the diocese: in 1099, Pope Urban II raised Braga to the status of a metropolitan see, and over the following century there began the long dispute between the archbishops of Braga and those of Santiago de Compostela over the ecclesiastical primacy of the Iberian Peninsula. In 1199, Pope Innocent III intervened in the dispute by granting Braga, as suffragans, the dioceses of Porto, Coimbra and Viseu, in addition to five other sees in what is today Spanish territory — a decision that gave rise to the title of Primate of the Spains, still borne today by the archbishop of Braga as a historical recognition of the precedence of the see of Braga over the others of Christian Iberia, even after Portugal consolidated itself as a kingdom independent of León and Castile.

The fabric of the cathedral grew by successive additions over almost a thousand years, which made it a true compendium of Portuguese religious architecture: from the original construction there remain Romanesque elements, such as the main portal and part of the naves; the 14th and 15th centuries added Gothic chapels and cloisters; the Manueline period, in the early 16th century, left its characteristic decorative mark on portals and altarpieces; and finally the Baroque of the 17th and 18th centuries covered parts of the interior, above all the main chapel and the upper choir, with gilded woodwork and monumental organs. Among its most venerated chapels is the Chapel of the Kings, a pantheon where Dom Henry of Burgundy and Dona Theresa of León, parents of the first king of Portugal, Dom Afonso Henriques, are buried; their tombs were commissioned only in the 16th century by Archbishop Dom Diogo de Sousa — reinforcing the symbolic bond between the cathedral and the very foundation of the Portuguese nation. It was also Dom Diogo de Sousa who, in the early 16th century, promoted the reconstruction of the cathedral's head (the apse area) in the Manueline style, commissioning the project from the architect João de Castilho in 1509 and building for himself, in the Chapel of Our Lady of Piety, a tomb now classified as a National Monument; the main chapel also preserves an altar frontal carved in Ançã stone, considered one of the most representative examples of Portuguese Manueline sculpture. In the upper choir, the old medieval choir stalls were replaced at the end of the 1730s by a Joanine Baroque ensemble with two levels of seats, with a cathedra reserved for the archbishop — one more layer, among so many, in the stylistic stratification that makes Braga Cathedral a rare continuous compendium of almost a thousand years of Portuguese religious art. The Cathedral also keeps one of the most important treasures of sacred art in the country, including pieces of medieval goldsmithing and one of the few Iberian Baroque organs still in regular use for liturgical celebrations. In 2024, the archdiocese and the city marked the 935th anniversary of the consecration of the church, reaffirming its role as the mother church of Catholicism in Portugal.

Among the most notable chapels of the complex is the Chapel of Saint Gerald, built in the 12th century as the funerary chapel of Archbishop Gerald, the first incumbent of the restored see after the Reconquista, and completely remodeled in the 18th century by Archbishop Dom Rodrigo de Moura Teles, who covered it with gilded woodwork and azulejos attributed to António de Oliveira Bernardes narrating episodes from the life of the saint. Two large Baroque organs, installed near the entrance of the church, bear witness to the importance that the Baroque period had in the musical and decorative history of the cathedral. Since 1930, part of the vast collection accumulated over almost a thousand years of Christian life around the Cathedral has been gathered in the Treasury-Museum, housed in the former Chapter House, an 18th-century building: the collection includes pieces of medieval and modern liturgical goldsmithing, embroidered priestly vestments, sculptures and documents that record the long history of the primatial archdiocese from the Middle Ages to the present day, establishing Braga Cathedral not only as a living place of worship, but as one of the main repositories of Portuguese sacred art.

Over two balconies raised above the central nave, the cathedral also preserves a rare set of two 18th-century Iberian pipe organs — the organ on the Gospel side, from 1737, and the one on the Epistle side, from 1739 —, both built by Simões Fontanes and framed by gilded woodwork by Marceliano de Araújo, forming one of the most highly valued sets of Baroque organs in Portugal for both their musical interest and the artistic value of their carved cases. Classified as a National Monument since the early 20th century, the Cathedral remains the active seat of the Archdiocese of Braga and the mother church of the largest ecclesiastical province in the country, gathering around itself, over the centuries, a good part of the religious, artistic and political history of northern Portugal.

itens.resumo: Metropolitan Cathedral of São Paulo, one of the largest Neo-Gothic churches in the world, built at the city's zero marker and the setting of central episodes in Brazilian civic life.
itens.corpo:
Officially the Metropolitan Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption and Saint Paul, the Sé Cathedral has occupied, since the 16th century, the site where the first mother church of the town of São Paulo de Piratininga was built, around 1589, on land that, according to tradition, was donated by the chief Tibiriçá. Raised to the status of an episcopal see in 1745, the church was replaced in 1764 by a new Baroque cathedral, which would stand until it was demolished in 1911. Already under the archdiocese created in 1908, Dom Duarte Leopoldo e Silva, the first Archbishop of São Paulo, decided to build on the site a cathedral befitting the city's rapid growth in the early 20th century. The project went to the German engineer Maximilian Emil Hehl, who settled in Brazil and conceived a predominantly Neo-Gothic building — although the dome over the crossing, inspired by the Italian Renaissance, introduces a hybrid stylistic note that is unusual among the great Neo-Gothic cathedrals of the world. Construction began in 1913 and progressed slowly for more than four decades, financed in part by fundraising campaigns among the Catholic community of São Paulo.

The inauguration, with the towers still unfinished, took place on January 25, 1954, deliberately coinciding with the celebrations of the fourth centenary of the founding of São Paulo. The twin towers, each 92 meters high, would only be completed in 1969. At 111 meters long and 46 meters wide, with a dome rising about 30 meters above the crossing, the cathedral can hold about eight thousand faithful and is considered one of the largest Neo-Gothic churches in the world, alongside landmarks such as the cathedrals of Cologne and Milan. More than 800 tons of rare marble were used in its construction, and the interior capitals were decorated with motifs of Brazilian fauna and flora — coffee branches, pineapples and armadillos — in a program that seeks to unite the Christian narrative with local memory.

The interior received about 750 square meters of stained glass of Italian and Brazilian manufacture, distributed across the naves, chapels and rose windows. The pipe organ, custom-built in Italy between 1953 and 1954 by the firm Balbiani & Rossi (Balbiani Vegezzi-Bosi), in Milan and Turin, arrived in Brazil through the port of Santos and was installed around the high altar, being inaugurated about ten months after the opening of the cathedral. With five keyboards, 124 stops and approximately 11,000 pipes, it is described as one of the largest organs in Latin America; damaged, it remained unused for more than two decades, and a restoration project, made possible by the Rouanet Law and including the shipment of its parts to the Mascioni workshop in northern Italy, has been set in motion to restore its sound. Beneath the floor of the cathedral, a large crypt under the high altar holds the tombs of all the bishops and archbishops of São Paulo and of figures from the history of São Paulo covered by exceptions to the rule: the chief Tibiriçá, an indigenous leader of the Guaianás tribe who first welcomed the Jesuits on the Piratininga plateau; Father Diogo Antônio Feijó, who served as regent of the Empire of Brazil during the minority of Dom Pedro II; and Father Bartolomeu Lourenço de Gusmão, a Portuguese-Brazilian inventor who pioneered experiments with hot-air balloons in the early 18th century.

Over the course of the 20th century, the square and the cathedral became the setting of central episodes in Brazilian political history. During the military dictatorship, Cardinal Archbishop Dom Paulo Evaristo Arns, who headed the archdiocese from 1970, turned the Sé into a space welcoming ecumenical demonstrations in defense of human rights. In October 1975, he celebrated in the cathedral the historic ecumenical service in memory of the journalist Vladimir Herzog, who was killed under torture by the regime, an event conducted alongside Rabbi Henry Sobel and Reverend Jaime Wright, in one of the greatest gestures of civil resistance of that period. On January 25, 1984, the city's anniversary, the Praça da Sé hosted one of the largest rallies of the Diretas Já movement, which demanded direct elections for president at the end of the military regime — gathering, according to estimates, between 300,000 and 400,000 people, with the presence of the main national opposition leaders, artists and representatives of civil society, consolidating the area around the cathedral as a symbolic stage of the country's return to democracy. The church underwent a major renovation between 2000 and 2002, when the original plans of 1912 were found inside the building itself, which allowed a faithful restoration of the structure. Seat of the Archdiocese of São Paulo — now led by Cardinal Dom Odilo Pedro Scherer — and located exactly at the city's zero marker, in the Praça da Sé, the cathedral remains one of the most recognizable urban and religious landmarks in Brazil.

itens.resumo: Circular cathedral of Brasília designed by Oscar Niemeyer, with structure by Joaquim Cardozo, the greatest symbol of Brazilian modern architecture.
itens.corpo:
The Metropolitan Cathedral of Our Lady of Aparecida, seat of the Archdiocese of Brasília, was designed by Oscar Niemeyer as part of the urban plan for the new capital, conceived alongside him by Lúcio Costa. Dedicated to the Virgin Mary under the title of Our Lady of Aparecida—proclaimed by the Church Queen and Patroness of Brazil—, its foundation stone was laid on September 12, 1958, still during the accelerated construction of Brasília under the government of Juscelino Kubitschek, but it was only officially inaugurated and dedicated to worship on May 31, 1970, a decade after the city's inauguration in 1960. The structure, calculated by the engineer and poet from Pernambuco Joaquim Cardozo—a longtime collaborator of Niemeyer on several works in the capital—, is made up of sixteen reinforced concrete columns of variable cross-section, each weighing about 90 tons, which rise at an incline from a circular base and cross at the top, giving the whole its characteristic shape of a crown of thorns or of hands joined in prayer, depending on each observer's interpretation. The number of columns, however, was not the one originally envisioned: Niemeyer at one point proposed twenty-one columns forty meters high, later reduced to sixteen for purely aesthetic reasons—a decision that required Cardozo to calculate a system of pillars with complex geometry and, in some sections, a hollow triangular profile.

Niemeyer himself described his intention that the cathedral should work "as a great sculpture, a religious idea, a moment of prayer," prioritizing sculptural and spatial impact over the traditional conventions of religious architecture. In the structural design, Cardozo resorted to solutions that were remarkable for the time, such as the tension ring that absorbs the horizontal forces transmitted by the columns, isolated from the infrastructure by neoprene plates that prevent the transmission of movements—as well as a study of the effect of wind loads on the stained glass windows in interaction with the pillars, a verification that was sophisticated by the technical standards of the day. The engineer also replaced the concrete band planned for the top with a slab positioned lower down, which gave the building a cleaner silhouette. At the highest point rests a metal cross twelve meters tall, blessed by Pope Paul VI. At the 1970 inauguration, the space between the columns was closed with clear glass; only in a renovation in 1987 did the French-born artist based in Brazil Marianne Peretti—the only woman on the original team of Niemeyer and Lúcio Costa for the construction of Brasília—replace those panels with her definitive stained glass windows, sixteen hand-painted glass panels in shades of blue, green, white and gold that now bathe the interior of the church in colored light. In a second restoration campaign, begun in 2000, the stained glass windows were restored with special glass from Milan that received a climate-control film, allowing light but not heat to pass through, and the reflecting pool that embraces the monument was waterproofed again, also contributing to the natural climate control of the environment.

Access to the main nave is by a descending ramp that leads visitors to an underground atrium before emerging into the circular space beneath the stained glass—a path that Niemeyer conceived as a symbolic passage from darkness to light. From the ceiling, three angels suspended by steel cables hover over the faithful: the smallest is 2.22 meters long and weighs 100 kilograms, the middle one measures 3.4 meters and weighs 200 kilograms, and the largest reaches 4.25 meters and about 300 kilograms, all the work of Alfredo Ceschiatti with the collaboration of Dante Croce, from 1970. In the outdoor square, the bronze sculptures of the Four Evangelists, also by Ceschiatti, greet visitors before this descent, flanking the access to the baptistery. The interior of the nave, with a capacity for about four thousand people, is lined with about 500 tons of marble, and the Way of the Cross is the work of Di Cavalcanti. On the main altar is the Eucharistic table in Carrara marble, donated by Pope Paul VI, a gesture that underscored the international significance attributed to the young Archdiocese of Brasília; beneath the main altar there is a small chapel accessible from each of its sides. Next to the altar, a replica of the image of Our Lady of Aparecida—whose original was found in the waters of the Paraíba do Sul River in the 18th century—is kept in a crystal case also designed by Niemeyer. On the outside, a freestanding bell tower about twenty meters high holds four large bells that mark the hours and call the faithful to celebrations.

Construction advanced in two very distinct phases: between 1959 and 1960, still at the accelerated pace of the inauguration of Brasília, only the structure of the sixteen concrete columns that form the main nave was erected, leaving for almost a decade the rest of the work—reflecting pool, baptistery, bell tower, interior finishing, sacristy and access ramp—to be completed only between 1969 and 1970, shortly before the official inauguration. The use of reinforced concrete as an exposed structural material, without coverings that would hide its monolithic quality, became one of the signatures of Niemeyer's mature style and has earned the Metropolitan Cathedral recurring academic studies on the relationship between structural form and the sensory experience of modern religious architecture. Besides being the archdiocesan seat, the cathedral serves a civic function: the inauguration ceremony of the President of the Republic traditionally begins there. Officially recognized as part of Brasília's urban ensemble—listed by the then National Historic and Artistic Heritage Service, today IPHAN, on November 19, 1991—, the cathedral is also part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing granted to the Brazilian capital in 1987, a recognition of the city's modernist architectural ensemble as one of the most complete and coherent of the 20th century. Together with this monumental ensemble, it was decisive in Niemeyer's receiving the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1988, the profession's most important award, of which the architect from Rio de Janeiro was the first Latin American winner.

itens.resumo: First cathedral built in the Americas, in the Colonial Zone of Santo Domingo, raised to a metropolitan see and primatial see of the continent by the bull Super Universas (1546).
itens.corpo:
With the official name of Holy Metropolitan Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady Saint Mary of the Incarnation — but popularly known as Santa María la Menor —, the Primatial Cathedral of America is the oldest Catholic cathedral in continuous operation in the New World. Its origin goes back to the bull Romanus Pontifex, of August 8, 1511, by which Pope Julius II created the Diocese of Santo Domingo — the first in the Americas —, a city founded by Nicolás de Ovando in 1502, after the first European settlement had been destroyed by a hurricane. A modest first cathedral began to be built on May 12, 1512, with walls of straw and wood, and the cornerstone was laid by the second bishop, Alessandro Geraldini. The plans, however, were entirely revised from 1520 onward, with the arrival of that same humanist bishop, who drove the construction of the present building, erected essentially between 1521 and 1537 under the direction of the Sevillian architect Luis de Moya and later of Rodrigo de Liendo, with interventions by Alonso González, inspired by the Cathedral of Seville. The work was consecrated in 1541 by Bishop Alonso de Fuenmayor, who dedicated it to Our Lady of the Incarnation. The result is a hybrid architecture, combining the late Gothic of the ribbed vaults with Plateresque, Renaissance and Herrerian elements — one of the first examples of European religious architecture built on American soil and a direct reference for later cathedrals throughout the continent. The church measures about 54 meters in length by 23 in width, with a ceiling of approximately 16 meters.

On February 12, 1546, at the request of King Charles I of Spain (the Emperor Charles V), Pope Paul III, by the bull Super Universas, raised the see of Santo Domingo to the rank of archdiocese, at the same time creating the first three archbishoprics of the New World — Santo Domingo, Mexico and Lima. Santo Domingo was then honored as the primatial see of the Indies, with the suffragan dioceses of La Concepción de la Vega, Puerto Rico, Cuba, Coro (Venezuela), Santa Marta and Cartagena (Colombia), Honduras and the abbey of Jamaica; New Orleans would be designated a suffragan on September 12, 1554. This title of Primatial Cathedral of the Americas was later ratified, according to documentary tradition, by the bull Divinis Praeceptis. The dignity of Minor Basilica would come only much later, on July 14, 1920, when Pope Benedict XV, by the brief Non Sine Secreto, granted the church the title.

The cathedral holds about fourteen side chapels, many funded by noble families of the colony and adorned with altars carved in wood and marble, as well as tombs of colonial administrators. Among the controversies that marked its history is a dramatic episode: in the summer of 1586, the English privateer Francis Drake — acting under the sponsorship of Queen Elizabeth I, who had financed him to "punish the King of Spain in his Indies" — invaded and occupied Santo Domingo. Informed of the fleet's arrival on January 10, the population fled carrying gold and jewels; after landing at Haina on January 11, the expedition of 23 ships and about 2,300 men set up its headquarters inside the cathedral itself, which also served as a warehouse and prison. The English plundered the city, burned ships and only left it on February 10, 1586, after receiving a ransom of 25,000 ducats, also carrying off the church bells, the artillery of the fortresses, hides, sugar and vessels.

Another historical dispute of great repercussion revolves around Christopher Columbus. In September 1877, during excavations in the cathedral, a lead urn was discovered whose lid bore the inscription "Ilustre y Esdo Varon Dn Cristóbal Colón"; the remains were said to have been brought from Spain as early as the sixteenth century by the vicereine María de Toledo, daughter of the Admiral. Transferred to Havana in 1795, when the Treaty of Basel ceded Santo Domingo to France, and later taken to the Cathedral of Seville in 1898, the remains of Columbus stayed in the Dominican church — from the end of the nineteenth century in a marble mausoleum by the Catalan sculptor Pedro Carbonell — until they were transferred, in 1992, to the monumental Columbus Lighthouse (Faro a Colombo), inaugurated on October 6 of that year in the presence of Pope John Paul II. The question of whether the authentic remains of the Admiral stayed in Santo Domingo or in Seville remains open: in 2006, the University of Granada confirmed by mitochondrial DNA analysis that the remains in Seville were authentic, but the Dominican authorities did not allow the same study to be done on those in the Faro a Colombo. The church also received three papal visits — John Paul II in 1979, 1984 and 1992, when he presided there over the Fourth General Conference of the Latin American Episcopate.

Located in the heart of the Colonial City of Santo Domingo — the first permanent European settlement in the Americas, founded by Bartholomew Columbus in 1496 and recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1990 —, the cathedral remains the seat of the Archdiocese of Santo Domingo and one of the main living historical monuments of the American continent, having undergone restoration work on its façade, roofs and buttresses in heritage conservation programs.

itens.titulo: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace of Yamoussoukro
itens.resumo: The largest Christian church in the world by built area, erected in the administrative capital of Ivory Coast on the initiative of President Félix Houphouët-Boigny and consecrated by Pope John Paul II in 1990.
itens.corpo:
The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace (in French, Basilique Notre-Dame de la Paix) is a Catholic minor basilica built in Yamoussoukro, the administrative capital of Ivory Coast since March 1983. It is not, however, the cathedral of the local diocese: that role belongs to the neighboring Cathedral of Saint Augustine, less than three kilometers away, the seat of the Bishop of Yamoussoukro — a distinction frequently overlooked by the public. It was built between August 10, 1985 — the date of the laying and blessing of the first stone — and 1989, on the personal initiative of Félix Houphouët-Boigny, president of the country since independence in 1960, who decided to transform his hometown into the new capital in place of Abidjan. Houphouët-Boigny personally chose the architects — the Lebanese-Ivorian Pierre Fakhoury and the Frenchman Patrick Hauthuille — and determined that the church should be inspired by Saint Peter's Basilica in the Vatican, while insisting that it surpass it in size. The dome, about 90 meters in diameter, is more than double that of Saint Peter's (41 meters), although it rests on a lower base, so that its final height — 158 meters, crowned by a large cross — is slightly greater than that of the Roman model.

The work mobilized thousands of workers from the region under the supervision of European technicians and engineers, bringing together 24 companies in its execution. The complex occupies about 130 hectares, with earthworks of 800,000 cubic meters and foundations of 156 concrete piles. The elliptical access esplanade, of about 30,000 square meters, is surrounded by 128 columns 21 meters high. The financing came directly from Houphouët-Boigny's personal coffers, but the real cost was never precisely disclosed: estimates range from 175 million to 600 million dollars, and there is no documentary consensus on the widely repeated claim that the higher figure would equal twice the country's entire foreign debt — a version that more recent sources consider unconfirmed by the original data. The contrast between the gigantic scale of the project and widespread poverty made the basilica, from the time of its construction, a controversial symbol, criticized inside and outside the country as a monument to the personal vanity of a head of state, at a time when Ivory Coast was facing an economic and fiscal crisis, with cities lacking running water and diseases spreading. The international press nicknamed it the "basilica in the jungle."

Pope John Paul II consecrated the church on September 10, 1990, after formally receiving the basilica as a gift from Houphouët-Boigny on behalf of the Catholic Church. The consecration came with an explicit condition: the construction, beside the basilica, of a hospital for the local population, as a social counterpart to the magnitude of the religious investment. The hospital, however, had its construction halted during the civil war and the Ivorian political-military crises from 2002 to 2011, and was only completed in 2014 and opened in January 2015, at a cost of about 21.3 million euros. The basilica is currently administered by Polish Pallottine priests, at an estimated annual cost of 1.5 million dollars, and alongside the church there are two identical buildings — a refectory and a residence reserved for papal visits, used only once.

Architecturally, the building reproduces on an enlarged scale central elements of Saint Peter's in the Vatican, with a dome, colonnade and vast access square; inside, it received about 8,400 square meters of contemporary stained glass, commissioned from the studio France Vitrail International of Paris — the largest stained glass order ever placed in the world, with about five thousand shades of glass — as well as marble imported from Italy, Spain and Portugal, in a cladding totaling about 700,000 square meters. Among the figures depicted in the stained glass is President Houphouët-Boigny himself, shown kneeling before Jesus, a gesture that reinforced criticism of the monumental and personalist character of the project. The total capacity is about 18,000 people — approximately 7,000 seated in the nave and 11,000 standing — far less than the 60,000 of Saint Peter's; even so, for most of the year the basilica records congregations of only a few hundred faithful, filling up chiefly on major liturgical dates such as Easter and Christmas. More than three decades after its consecration, the church continues to be described as one of the emptiest on the planet in the ordinary liturgical calendar — a contrast that has made it a recurring object of study on the limits between devotion, architectural monumentality and personal political power in post-colonial Africa.
fontes: Dédicace de la Basilique Notre-Dame de la Paix, official communiqué, 1990 (cited in the English Wikipedia)

itens.resumo: The principal Catholic church of England and Wales, built in London in the Neo-Byzantine style so as not to be confused with the neighboring Anglican Westminster Abbey.
itens.corpo:
The Metropolitan Cathedral of the Most Precious Blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ — known simply as Westminster Cathedral — is the seat of the Archdiocese of Westminster and the principal Catholic church of England and Wales. Its history is tied to the restoration of the English Catholic hierarchy in 1850, when Pope Pius IX reestablished bishops and archbishops in the country after centuries of persecution and legal restrictions dating from the Reformation under Henry VIII; for this reason, the Catholic Church was still viewed with suspicion by part of British society at the time. The land on which the church stands, a few steps from the Anglican Westminster Abbey, was acquired in 1884 — when the Archbishop of Westminster was Cardinal Henry Edward Manning — and had been, until 1877, the site of the Tothill Fields Bridewell prison (also called Tothill Fields Prison), which was closed that year and demolished in 1885; the foundations of the old prison were reused in the new construction. It was Cardinal Herbert Vaughan, the third Archbishop of Westminster since 1892, who carried forward the project of giving English Catholicism a cathedral worthy of the capital of the empire, commissioning it, without a public competition, from the architect John Francis Bentley, with a clear instruction: the new Catholic church should not resemble the Anglican abbey, with its medieval Gothic tradition, so as to avoid confusion of identities and direct stylistic competition. The decision to dispense with a competition and hire an architect little known outside Catholic circles provoked protests from other architects, but Vaughan stood by his choice.

Bentley responded with a Neo-Byzantine design, inspired above all by St Mark's in Venice, San Vitale in Ravenna and Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, an aesthetic choice then unusual in England, which suggested a Roman Catholicism with roots predating the Anglican split itself. In November 1894 he set out for Italy in search of references, passing through Milan, Pavia, Pisa, Naples and Rome; he was unable to go to Constantinople because of an outbreak of cholera. He disliked the Baroque style of Saint Peter's, and rejected the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, preferred by Vaughan — who wanted an Early Christian style. Bentley imposed his version of the Byzantine, with the declared intention of "developing, as far as possible, the first phase of Christian architecture"; Vaughan yielded on the style, but rejected the original plan for two towers, saying that "one would be enough for me". The result was a large building of exposed brick, with horizontal bands of white Portland stone and no internal steel reinforcement — a more economical and quicker solution, which deliberately exposed the texture of the material on the red-and-white striped façade that became the visual signature of the church. Bentley was proud of having conceived a structure of that size solely with brick, stone and concrete.

Work began in 1895: the foundation stone was blessed on 29 June of that year. The building was architecturally complete in 1903, the year it was opened for worship, but Bentley did not live to see it finished, having died in 1902 — one of the first services celebrated in the church was precisely the funeral of Cardinal Vaughan, who also died shortly after the opening. The official liturgical consecration only took place on 28 June 1910, postponed until the debt incurred for the construction had been fully paid off, in accordance with the canonical norm that reserves full consecration for churches free of financial encumbrances. The façade is dominated by the bell tower, the Tower of Saint Edward, about 87 meters high including the cross — which at the top encloses a relic of the True Cross — and a viewing gallery open to the public.

The interior preserves a deliberate contrast with the monumentality of the exterior. By decision of Bentley and his successors, the decoration in Byzantine mosaics — one of the most ambitious elements of the project — advanced only partially over the course of the twentieth century, financed exclusively by donations specific to each chapel, so that parts of the ceiling and walls still remain in bare brick awaiting future donors, in a process that those responsible describe as purposely open-ended and without a deadline, like the medieval cathedrals completed over the course of centuries. Among the areas already finished, the Chapel of the Blessed Sacrament and the Chapel of Saint Andrew stand out, with mosaics of rich golden polychromy. The cathedral is renowned for its musical tradition: Cardinal Vaughan founded, at the very inauguration, a choir of its own under the direction of the first master of music, Richard Runciman Terry, who would become an international reference in the rediscovery and performance of Renaissance sacred polyphony. This tradition is maintained to this day by the Westminster Cathedral Choir School, a Catholic preparatory school for boys that trains the resident choristers: the boys rehearse before and after classes and sing seven liturgical services a week, keeping alive one of the few boys' choir traditions still active on a daily basis in Europe. The liturgical routine includes Vespers and sung Mass from Monday to Friday, Mass in Latin on Saturdays, and Solemn Mass with Vespers and Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament on Sundays, making Westminster Cathedral one of the most active centers of sacred music in the English-speaking Catholic world.

itens.resumo: Seat of the Archdiocese of New York and the largest neo-Gothic Catholic cathedral in the United States, built on Fifth Avenue across from Rockefeller Center.
itens.corpo:
St. Patrick's Cathedral was born of the vision of John Hughes, the first Archbishop of New York and a central figure in the consolidation of Catholicism—then made up mostly of Irish and German immigrants—in the nineteenth-century city. In 1850, Hughes announced his intention to build a cathedral “worthy of the greatness of this metropolis,” choosing for it a site then considered peripheral and far from the urban center, at the time occupied by a cemetery and distant from the commercial core of Manhattan—a decision that the newspapers of the day mocked as “Hughes's Folly,” given the cost of the undertaking and the then little-valued location. The cornerstone was laid in 1858, with a design by the architect James Renwick Jr., a New Yorker who was self-taught in architecture and who had already designed Grace Church and the original Smithsonian building in Washington. Work advanced for several years until it was suspended in the early 1860s because of the American Civil War, resuming only at the end of the conflict.

Completed in 1878 and solemnly dedicated on May 25, 1879, the cathedral required more than a million bricks in its construction, covered on the outside with white marble from the region. The two twin towers of the main façade, about 100 meters high, were only added in 1888, ten years after the completion of the main body—an addition that Renwick had already foreseen in the original design but that only became financially feasible later. Conceived in the neo-Gothic style inspired by the great French and German cathedrals, with pinnacles, rose windows, buttresses, and gargoyles typical of the European Gothic repertoire, it became, upon its completion, the largest neo-Gothic Catholic cathedral in North America, a status it retains to this day. Around it, the archbishop's residence and the rectory, also designed by Renwick, were added in the early 1880s.

Located on Fifth Avenue, between 50th and 51st Streets in Manhattan, directly across from the Rockefeller Center complex—built decades after the cathedral and today its most immediate modern architectural counterpoint—St. Patrick's Cathedral has become one of the most photographed and recognizable buildings in the New York cityscape, its white Gothic profile standing out amid the surrounding skyscrapers. Seat of the Archdiocese of New York, it is a regular venue for major public celebrations, official ceremonies, and funerals of American officials and public figures—among them the funeral of Senator Robert F. Kennedy in 1968, whose casket traveled from there by train to the burial at Arlington National Cemetery. In the months following the attacks of September 11, 2001, the cathedral hosted dozens of funerals and Masses in memory of the firefighters and police officers killed in the attack on the World Trade Center, a role that reinforced its symbolic place in the civic life of the city. Designated a National Historic Landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places of the United States on December 8, 1976, the cathedral underwent an extensive structural restoration between 2012 and 2015, at a cost of about 177 million dollars, which cleaned decades of accumulated pollution from its marble façade, restored the stained-glass windows, and completely overhauled the main organ and the lighting system, without ever interrupting the continuous liturgical use of the church—the work was completed only a few days before Pope Francis's visit to the cathedral in September 2015.

Among the most admired artistic elements of the interior is the great rose window of the main façade, almost eight meters in diameter, designed by the American stained-glass master Charles Connick and made up of about three thousand pieces of hand-cut glass, considered one of the masterpieces of twentieth-century American stained glass. Below it stands the cathedral's great organ, installed in 1930 by the Kilgen company with 7,855 pipes ranging from a little over one centimeter to almost ten meters in length. Behind the high altar, the Lady Chapel, completed in 1900 according to a design by Charles T. Mathews, holds English stained-glass windows installed over two and a half decades and an image of the Virgin Mary; nearby there is also a Pietà sculpted in 1906 by the American sculptor William O. Partridge, three times larger than Michelangelo's Pietà in Saint Peter's Basilica in the Vatican.

The choice of the neo-Gothic style and the monumental scale of Renwick's design reflected Hughes's ambition to prove, through architecture, that Catholicism—practiced mostly by the poor Irish and German immigrants then arriving in New York en masse—had a place of prominence and permanence in the life of the city, in a context of strong nativist and anti-Catholic prejudice in the nineteenth-century United States. The location, initially ridiculed as peripheral, became, a few decades later, one of the most valuable in Manhattan, and the cathedral today rises surrounded by corporate skyscrapers, forming a visual contrast that sums up much of New York's own urban history—the endurance of a nineteenth-century religious landmark in the financial and commercial heart of the twenty-first century.

itens.resumo: One of only three churches in the world built over the tomb of an apostle, in India, where tradition places the martyrdom of Saint Thomas.
itens.corpo:
According to the tradition of the Saint Thomas Christians of India — a community that, by its own historical memory, goes back to the first centuries of Christianity —, the Apostle Thomas landed on the Malabar coast, in southwestern India, around the year 52, where he is said to have founded seven Christian communities still revered today by that Church. According to the same tradition, Thomas later crossed the subcontinent to the eastern coast, in the region of present-day Chennai (formerly Madras), where he preached and was martyred around the year 72, pierced by a lance while praying in a cave nearby — today also a pilgrimage site known as Saint Thomas Mount. His body is said to have been buried at the place where the Basilica of Saint Thomas now stands, in Mylapore, making the church one of only three in the world built directly over the tomb of one of the Twelve Apostles, alongside Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, over the tomb of Peter, and the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, in Spain, associated with the tradition of the burial of James the Greater.

The Christian presence in Mylapore endured for centuries without any link to Europe: historical records indicate that, as early as the 9th and 10th centuries, Arab travelers called the city Betumah ("city of Thomas"), and that communities of Nestorian Christians from Persia maintained a center of worship there. Marco Polo himself, in his travels in the East between 1254 and 1324, visited the site and recorded in his accounts the existence of a small chapel built over the tomb of the apostle, which had by then been an object of veneration for generations by local Christians as well as by Muslims and Hindus of the region, who recognized the holiness of the place regardless of their own religious tradition. When the Portuguese arrived on the Coromandel coast in the early 16th century, in search of the apostle's relics mentioned in medieval European accounts, they found the ancient chapel already in ruins; they rebuilt it in 1523 as a stone church, beginning the organized Catholic presence in the region under the sphere of influence of the Portuguese Padroado in the East.

The building seen today, in neo-Gothic style with a white tower about 47 meters high visible from the sea, is the result of an extensive reconstruction carried out between 1893 and 1896 under British administration of the Madras province, when the old Portuguese church was replaced by a larger church, European in inspiration but built on the same historic foundations. Pope Pius XII elevated the church to the dignity of minor basilica in 1956, a recognition renewed and expanded over the following century through successive visits by international ecclesiastical authorities. One of the most visited features of the complex is the underground crypt, reached by a narrow staircase, where pilgrims can approach the place traditionally identified as the tomb of the apostle, marked by an image of Saint Thomas and by relics associated with the lance of his martyrdom; nearby, a small museum houses archaeological finds from the region, including ancient Roman coins found in excavations nearby, evidence of trade routes between the Roman Empire and the Indian coast as early as the first centuries of the Christian era. The basilica remains today one of the main Christian pilgrimage destinations in Asia, receiving faithful from the Catholic, Syriac Orthodox and Protestant traditions, all claiming some historical connection with the evangelization of Thomas in the Indian subcontinent.

The current neo-Gothic reconstruction, solemnly consecrated on April 1, 1896 by Bishop Henry Reed of the diocese of Madras, gave the basilica its white tower, now visible from a great distance at sea and historically also used as a landmark by navigators approaching the Coromandel coast. In the museum attached to the church, visitors can see relics associated with the tradition of the apostle's death, among them a lance pointed out by local devotion as the instrument of his martyrdom, as well as archaeological pieces recovered in the region throughout the 20th century. In February 1986, Pope John Paul II visited the basilica during his journey to India — to this day the only Roman pontiff to make a pilgrimage to the tomb of Thomas in Mylapore —, a gesture that strengthened, before the universal Church, the recognition of the antiquity and importance of the Indian Christian tradition linked to the apostle.

The sixteen stained-glass windows and thirty-four colored glass panels that illuminate the interior of the church were commissioned from the historic Mayer & Company studio of Munich, Germany, and include, in a prominent arch behind the high altar, the scene most associated with the identity of the apostle: the Gospel episode in which Thomas, incredulous before the announcement of the Resurrection, touches with his finger the wound in Christ's side before professing his faith. Besides the lance of the martyrdom, the basilica's collection of relics also includes bone remains attributed to the apostle himself, preserved in a modern underground chapel, alongside relics of Saint Francis Xavier and of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, bringing together in one space material witnesses of different moments of the evangelization of Asia.

itens.resumo: The Cathedral of Santa Maria Nascente (Saint Mary of the Nativity), the Duomo of Milan, is the largest church in Italy and one of the largest Gothic cathedrals in the world. Its construction spanned more than six centuries, from 1386 until the installation of the last doors in the twentieth century, and it is the mother church of all the faithful of the Ambrosian Rite.
itens.corpo:
Milan Cathedral, dedicated to the Nativity of Mary (Santa Maria Nascente), stands in the Piazza del Duomo on the site where the ancient cathedral of Santa Maria Maggiore and the Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio once stood. Construction began in 1386 under the patronage of the lord of Milan, Gian Galeazzo Visconti, who the following year, in 1387, established the Veneranda Fabbrica del Duomo, an institution still active today and responsible for the conservation of the church — a notable fact for a church that, as such, is independent of the Holy See in its administration.

The project deliberately adopted the Gothic style then in vogue in Europe, departing from the Lombard Romanesque traditions. Over the centuries, architects and artists of many generations worked on the building; the dome was the subject of studies attributed to Leonardo da Vinci's stay in Milan. The church was only completed in 1965, with the installation of the last doors, the result of a collective effort that spanned the Middle Ages, the Renaissance and the modern era.

The liturgical history of the Duomo records significant milestones. In 1418, Pope Martin V consecrated the high altar of the old Milanese cathedral. On October 20, 1577, Archbishop Saint Charles Borromeo consecrated the present building, establishing the solemnity of the Dedication of the Duomo. It was also Charles Borromeo who, after the Council of Trent, saved the Ambrosian Rite from extinction, reforming its liturgical books and founding the Congregation of the Ambrosian Rite. For this reason, the Dedication of the Duomo is now celebrated in the third week of October and gives its name to the liturgical period preceding Advent in Milan's own calendar.

Atop the tallest spire, at 108.5 meters, stands the gilded statue of the Madonnina, placed there in 1774, which has become a symbol of the city. The building covers an area of about 11,700 square meters, with an estimated capacity of 40,000 people, and is supported by an impressive forest of 135 spires and more than 3,400 statues. Among its relics, the cathedral keeps the so-called "ark" containing the remains of Saint Charles Borromeo.

itens.resumo: The Patriarchal Cathedral Basilica of Saint Mark in Venice houses the relics of Mark the Evangelist, brought from Alexandria in the ninth century. With its blend of Byzantine, Romanesque and Gothic forms and its golden mosaics, it is one of the most singular churches in Christendom.
itens.corpo:
St Mark's Basilica was born from an episode that would change the history of Venice: according to medieval chronicles, around 828-829 two Venetian merchants removed the body of Saint Mark the Evangelist from Alexandria, in Egypt — except for the head — and brought it to the lagoon. The relics were first placed in a tower of the castrum, the doge's fortified residence, until Doge Giustiniano Participazio ordained in his will the building of a church dedicated to the evangelist. Connected with this is the promotion of Saint Mark to patron of Venice, replacing the Greek Saint Theodore, and one more step in the city's autonomy from Byzantium.

The first church was built beginning around 829 and was sufficiently advanced by around 836 to receive the relics. The present building, with a Greek-cross plan and five domes, was rebuilt mainly from the eleventh century onward: at its consecration on October 8, 1094, it already had its essential form. The church combines Byzantine, Romanesque and Gothic elements, the result of successive building campaigns and of decorations accumulated over centuries.

The western façade was covered, at the end of the thirteenth century, with marbles, mosaics and trophies brought from Constantinople, among them the famous four bronze horses. The interior, covered by more than 8,000 square meters of mosaics on a golden ground, earned the basilica the nickname "Church of Gold." In 1807, St Mark's replaced the old cathedral of San Pietro di Castello as the episcopal see, becoming the cathedral church of the Patriarchate of Venice.

Today the basilica is part of the monumental complex of Piazza San Marco, beside the Doge's Palace, and the historic center of Venice and its lagoon have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. Among its treasures, the basilica preserves both the relics of the evangelist — partly returned by the Coptic Church in 1968 — and the famous Pala d'Oro, the altarpiece of gold and enamel that adorns the high altar.

itens.resumo: The Cathedral of Notre-Dame de Chartres, about 80 km southwest of Paris, is considered the zenith of French Gothic art. Rebuilt after the fire of 1194, it preserves one of the most complete ensembles of medieval stained glass in the world and the relic known as the Sancta Camisa.
itens.corpo:
Chartres Cathedral stands on an ancient sacred site: at least five cathedrals have succeeded one another there since the formation of the diocese in the 4th century. The earlier Romanesque building, associated with Bishop Fulbert, was struck by fires in 1134 and, decisively, on June 10, 1194, when a lightning bolt started a great fire. The exact extent of the damage is debated — the fact that the lead cames of the western windows survived suggests that contemporary accounts may have exaggerated the devastation — but the opportunity was seized to rebuild the choir and nave in the newest Gothic style.

The reconstruction took place mainly between 1194 and 1220, incorporating the western towers and façade that had escaped the fire. The result is a landmark of High Gothic: the cathedral has the widest nave of any cathedral in France, and its three-level elevation — arcade, triforium and clerestory — creates a luminous contour that leads the eye to the altar. The flying buttresses, essential to support these heights, made it possible to greatly enlarge the surfaces of stained glass.

Chartres preserves about 176 stained-glass windows, largely from the 13th century, which makes it one of the most complete and best-preserved ensembles of medieval glasswork in Europe. Among its jewels are the window of "Notre-Dame de la Belle Verrière," with the Virgin in blue, and the great north, south and west rose windows. On the floor, a stone labyrinth about 12 meters in diameter, walked by the faithful on pilgrimage, recalls the tradition of medieval pilgrimages.

The most celebrated relic is the Sancta Camisa, a tunic that tradition associates with the Virgin Mary and which is said to have been given to the cathedral by Charles the Bald. Its rediscovery after the fire of 1194, supposedly protected by priests behind iron doors, fueled the Marian devotion that made Chartres one of the greatest pilgrimage centers in France. The cathedral, dedicated to Our Lady, is still a pilgrimage destination today and was inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1979.

itens.resumo: St. Peter's Basilica, in Vatican City State, is the largest church of Catholicism and one of the four papal major basilicas. Built over the tomb of the Apostle Peter and constructed between 1506 and 1626, it is the work of Bramante, Michelangelo, Maderno and Bernini.
itens.corpo:
St. Peter's Basilica stands in Vatican City State, on the site where tradition places the tomb of the Apostle Peter, martyred in Rome. In the fourth century the Emperor Constantine had a great basilica built there, completed around 329, which during the Middle Ages was the main pilgrimage destination of the West and remained standing for more than a thousand years until it was demolished to make way for the present building.

Construction of the Renaissance basilica began on April 18, 1506, under the pontificate of Julius II, and was only completed on November 18, 1626, when Pope Urban VIII consecrated it. Some of the greatest names in Western art worked on the project: Donato Bramante, who conceived the centralized plan; Michelangelo, designer of the dome; Carlo Maderno, who lengthened the nave and designed the façade, built between 1607 and 1612; and Gian Lorenzo Bernini, responsible for the bronze baldachin over the main altar (1624-1633) and for the design of Saint Peter's Square with its colonnade.

The interior, of monumental proportions, covers about 23,000 square meters, with a dome that reaches 136.6 meters in height and 42 meters in diameter, and can hold tens of thousands of people. Among the works of art it houses are Michelangelo's Pietà and Bernini's baldachin, as well as the funerary monuments of numerous popes. The basilica also preserves the Chair of Saint Peter and the Holy Door, opened only in jubilee years.

The classification as a major basilica gives St. Peter's precedence over all the minor basilicas of the world, although, unlike the other papal major basilicas, it is located within the territory of the very State that is the seat of the papacy. Its primacy is, however, spiritual and ceremonial: the cathedral of the Bishop of Rome is the Basilica of Saint John Lateran. St. Peter's is the site of most papal ceremonies, from canonizations to great Masses, and, together with Vatican City, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.

itens.resumo: The 'Church of Holy Wisdom,' cathedral of Byzantine Constantinople, completed by Justinian in 537 and the largest cathedral in the world for almost a thousand years; its dome inaugurated the full use of the pendentive and is considered the supreme landmark of Byzantine architecture.
itens.corpo:
The Hagia Sophia (in Greek, 'Holy Wisdom,' a title that designates Christ himself, the second person of the Trinity; in Turkish, Ayasofya) stands in the Fatih district of Istanbul, on the site where three churches have succeeded one another since the fourth century. The first, dedicated in 360 during the reign of Constantius II, and the second, of 415, were destroyed by fires; after the Nika revolt in 532, Emperor Justinian I decided to build a temple without precedent. He entrusted the project to two men trained as mechanikoi — theorists of geometry and mechanics, not ordinary master masons: Anthemius of Tralles, author of treatises on conic sections, and Isidore of Miletus, editor of Archimedes. The work was erected in only about five years, from 532 to 537.

The great technical achievement of the Hagia Sophia is the central dome set upon pendentives — the geometric device in the form of a curved triangle that makes the transition from a square base to the circle of the dome, transmitting the weight to the four great piers. With a diameter of approximately 31 to 33 meters and its crown about 55 meters above the floor, the dome has at its base a crown of forty windows that makes it seem to float on light. The original structure, of brick and mortar over stone, suffered collapses: the first dome, too shallow, fell after an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt by Isidore the Younger between 558 and 562, taking on its present form, higher and ribbed. The building measures about 82 meters in length by 73 in width, and brings together materials from throughout the empire. Its interior decoration of gold, marbles and mosaics earned it the reputation of having 'changed the history of architecture.'

As the cathedral of Byzantine Constantinople and seat of the ecumenical patriarchate, the Hagia Sophia was the central temple of Greek Christendom from 537 until 1453, except for the interruption from 1204 to 1261, when the Latin crusaders of the Fourth Crusade imposed Catholic worship there. For almost a thousand years it remained the largest cathedral in the world, until it was surpassed by the completion of the Cathedral of Seville, in the early sixteenth century. The great imperial liturgies took place there; the poet Paul the Silentiary composed a famous description (ekphrasis) for its rededication in 562.

After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II converted the temple into a mosque, adding minarets and Islamic elements to it, and the figurative mosaics were gradually covered with plaster or whitewash. In 1934 a decree of the government of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk ended its religious use; the Hagia Sophia opened as a museum in 1935, when the Byzantine mosaics were revealed again. On July 10, 2020, the Turkish Council of State annulled that decree and a new presidential decree reopened the building to Muslim worship, with the first prayers held on July 24, 2020 — a decision contested by Christian authorities and by UNESCO. The complex has been part of the World Heritage Site 'Historic Areas of Istanbul' since 1985.

itens.resumo: French Gothic cathedral where 25 kings of France were crowned, from Louis VIII (1223) to Charles X (1825), including the coronation of Charles VII in 1429 in the presence of Joan of Arc; a masterpiece of High Gothic and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991.
itens.corpo:
The Cathedral of Notre-Dame de Reims, in the French city of Reims, on the banks of the Vesle River, is the seat of the Archdiocese of Reims and one of the most important works of Gothic architecture. The site has ancient roots: according to tradition, Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptized there at the end of the 5th century, which made Reims, for centuries, the natural setting for the coronation of the French monarchs. The present building began in 1211, under Archbishop Aubry de Humbert and the architect Jean d'Orbais, to replace the earlier church destroyed by a fire in 1210; the design was inspired by Chartres Cathedral (begun around 1194).

The main construction work extended over about eighty years, under the direction of four successive architects, with additions and decorative work continuing for centuries; the Gothic body is generally considered to have been completed within the 13th century, with the west façade flanked by two towers about 68 meters high, raised between 1210 and 1250. The cathedral is about 149 meters long by 130 meters deep in its interior plan, with a ceiling approximately 35 meters high. Its monumental sculpture — including the portals with the Visitation and the gallery of the kings of the Old Testament on the façade — is a landmark of Gothic art. The present central spire was added in the 19th-century restoration, replacing the original, which was removed in the 18th century because of instability.

Reims was the stage for 25 coronations of kings of France, from Louis VIII in 1223 to Charles X in 1825. The most famous took place in 1429, when Charles VII was crowned in the presence of Joan of Arc, a decisive episode of the Hundred Years' War. The church also preserves the memory of Saint John Baptist de La Salle, who celebrated his first Mass there in 1678.

The cathedral suffered grave damage when the German Imperial Army deliberately bombarded it in 1914, at the beginning of the First World War, in an attempt to strike French morale; the restoration was carried out in the 20th century, with the support of donors such as the American John D. Rockefeller. Franco-German reconciliation was symbolized at the site in July 1962, when President Charles de Gaulle and Chancellor Konrad Adenauer met there. On September 26, 1996, John Paul II visited Reims on the occasion of the 1500th anniversary of the baptism of Clovis. Since 1991, the cathedral, the former Abbey of Saint-Remi and the Palace of Tau have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage List.
